explanation: Store a composite flag for each integer through n. An unmarked candidate is prime: emit it and mark its multiples beginning at its square. Starting at p² avoids work already done by smaller prime factors.
timeComplexity: O(n log log n) for n≥3: initialization and the candidate scan cost O(n), while marking over primes costs O(n Σ(1/p)) = O(n log log n). Smaller inputs take constant time.
spaceComplexity: O(n) including n+1 composite flags and the returned primes. Compressing odd candidates improves the constant, not the asymptotic bound.
attribution: JavaScript port of the independently authored EPI Practice C# algorithm; no upstream reference code copied.
correctness: Every composite integer has a prime factor no larger than its square root. Before a candidate p is reached, every composite with a smaller prime factor has therefore been marked; an unmarked p is prime. Multiples below p² have a smaller prime factor and need no new marking. Marking from p² excludes every remaining composite divisible by p. Scanning candidates in increasing order returns each prime once and in sorted order.
walkthrough: For n=12, emit 2 and mark 4,6,8,10,12. Emit 3 and mark 9. Candidates 5,7 and 11 remain unmarked; each has square above 12. Skip all marked candidates and return [2,3,5,7,11].
edgeCases: The upper bound is inclusive: n=2 returns [2].
Begin marking at p², not p, or a prime would eliminate itself.
